rationale: A wins because it turns the same announcement into four clean desks: P&L, moat strategy, driver experience, and connector infrastructure. Its best line, "An unprofitable automaker just turned its charging network into a revenue line," is a real markets story with the proof burden named instead of perfume sprayed on. B has usable bones, but "Rivian fields a rival to Tesla's Supercharger network — without a single automaker partner to show for it" drags in a rivalry and failure frame the update does not give it.
gaps_in_A: "The prevailing belief: a proprietary fast-charging network is a moat" is outside the supplied facts; source that industry premise or frame it as a question.
"Every other EV driver just gained 3,500 fast chargers" may overstate practical access; compatibility, geography, and app flow need proof before saying every driver gained anything.

"Rivian just bet that an exclusive charging network isn't worth keeping" is a strong read, but it risks treating monetization as the whole motive unless Rivian will confirm exclusivity was not driving sales.
gaps_in_B: "following the industry's shift away from automaker-exclusive plugs" turns one company announcement into a trend without evidence in the update.
"newest brand-agnostic fast-charging grid" overclaims category status; the facts say Rivian opened 3,500+ chargers, not that it created or joined a defined grid category.
"Rivian fields a rival to Tesla's Supercharger network" invents a Tesla-rival positioning the update never states.
"without a single automaker partner to show for it" weaponizes "no partnership announced" into a failure frame; that's editorial seasoning, not grounding.
